fullPassage: A person, let's call him Opt (for optimist), never goes to the doctor and feels healthy. Opt will likely have nothing to worry about until later in life—perhaps until it is too late. Yet, until that time, Opt can claim that he is healthy and that he has nothing to worry about. A friend of his, Caut (for cautious), is more proactive. He regularly visits the doctor from an early age, and, as soon as he realizes that his blood pressure is above the normal range, he starts losing weight and exercising more than before. Caut starts feeling awkward because he cannot eat and drink as much as his friend Opt, and he has to walk to work in order to exercise. Opt even makes fun of him, calling him an imaginary patient. Should Caut feel embarrassed? No! Caut is doing what he can to lead a better life in the long term; he is self-correcting his life habits. Opt has left things to chance and does not worry if he does harm to his body. Science is like Caut, not Opt: it is a self-correcting enterprise that aims for the best possible condition. It's not embarrassed to correct itself, unlike other enterprises that are either unaware of their problems or prefer to live in eternal ignorance. This self-awareness and self-correcting aspect of science provides a good reason to trust it despite its failings. As it was nicely put recently: The discovery that an experiment does not replicate is not a lack of success but an opportunity. Many of the current concerns about reproducibility represent the dynamic, iterative nature of the process of discovery where discordant results are essential to producing more integrated accounts and (eventually) translation. A failure to reproduce is only the first step in scientific inquiry. In many ways, how science responds to these failures is what determines whether it succeeds.

questions.passage:
(A) Caut is doing what he can to <u>lead</u> a better life in the long term; he is self-correcting his life habits.

(B) An experienced captain must <u>lead</u> the whole crew safely through the storm.
questions.stem: 다음 (A)와 (B)의 밑줄 친 lead의 문맥적 의미로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: (A) lead a life = (삶을) 영위하다, 살다 / (B) lead the crew = (사람들을) 이끌다, 인솔하다
det.analysis:
❌ ① (A) 이끌다 — (B) 영위하다: (A)는 'lead a better life(더 나은 삶을 살다)'이므로 '이끌다'가 아님
✅ ② (A) (삶을) 영위하다 — (B) 이끌다: (A) lead a life=삶을 영위하다, (B) lead the crew=선원들을 이끌다 ←정답
❌ ③ (A) 영위하다 — (B) (금속) 납: (B)는 선원을 '이끈다'는 동사이지 금속 '납'이 아님
❌ ④ (A) 안내하다 — (B) 영위하다: (A)·(B) 뜻이 뒤바뀜
det.tip: lead a life = 삶을 영위하다(살다) / lead + 사람 = ~을 이끌다. 문맥으로 구별

questions.stem: 다음 영영 정의에 해당하는 단어로 가장 적절한 것은? "to copy something exactly, or to produce the same result again"

det.analysis:
❌ ① translate(번역하다) — 언어를 옮기는 것
❌ ② represent(나타내다) — 대표하거나 표현하는 것
❌ ③ respond(반응하다) — 반응·대응하는 것
✅ ④ replicate(복제·재현하다) — 똑같이 복제하거나 같은 결과를 다시 만들어 내는 것 ←정답
det.tip: replicate = 복제하다, 재현하다. an experiment does not replicate = 실험이 재현되지 않는다

questions.passage: A friend of his, Caut (for cautious), is more proactive. He regularly visits the doctor from an early age, and, as soon as he realizes that his blood pressure is above the normal range, he starts __________ (lose) weight and exercising more than before.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 괄호 안의 단어를 알맞은 형태로 바꿔 쓰시오. (1단어, 영어로)

det.korean: start 뒤에는 동명사(-ing)가 와요. lose → losing. 뒤의 exercising과 병렬
det.analysis: start + V-ing: '~하기 시작하다'. start 뒤 동사는 동명사(-ing)가 되어야 하고, 뒤에 나오는 exercising과도 and로 병렬 연결돼요. lose(줄이다) → losing
det.tip: start losing weight = 체중 감량을 시작하다. start 뒤 동명사, exercising과 병렬

questions.passage: Caut is doing what he can to lead a better life in the long term; he is self-correcting his life habits. Opt has __________ (leave) things to chance and does not worry if he does harm to his body.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 괄호 안의 단어를 알맞은 형태로 바꿔 쓰시오. (1단어, 영어로)

det.korean: has + 과거분사 = 현재완료. leave의 과거분사는 불규칙형 left
det.analysis: has + p.p.(과거분사) = 현재완료. '지금까지 ~해 왔다'는 의미예요. leave는 불규칙 동사라 과거분사가 leaved가 아니라 left. Opt has left things to chance = Opt은 일을 운에 맡겨 왔다
det.tip: has left = 현재완료(has + p.p.). leave의 과거분사는 불규칙형 left
